en: The Mahāyāna Scripture on Revealing Consciousness, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of Central India by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

In the forest, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions and had attained mastery; whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; who possessed unimpeded illumination regarding the past, future, and present; who were great nāgas;

who, according to the Buddha’s teaching, had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, achieved their own benefit, and severed the suffering of existence within the cycle of birth and death; and who, by the power of right knowledge, well understood the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings—such was this assembly of great śrāvakas, with the Elder Śāriputra as their leader.
Furthermore, there was an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered together in that assembly.

At that time, many of the bhikṣus were present with the World-Honored One; they were overcome by fatigue and drowsiness, their composure lost and their bodies slumped so that they could not support themselves.
Thereupon, the radiance from the World-Honored One’s countenance shone forth like a blooming lotus flower.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were fully awakened; each became solemn and composed, and they thought to themselves:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has a countenance so radiant and a face so luminous—what Dharma-eye does he wish to open to bring great benefit?"

At that time, the youth Bhadrapāla, of supreme excellence, possessed a refined and magnificent countenance, endowed with a soft, radiant luster and perfect physical marks; surrounded by sixty thousand merchant leaders, his retinue’s tumultuous clamor was like the shaking of the earth, he approached the place where the Buddha was.

Beholding the Buddha, the World-Honored One—the treasury of all virtues, serene and secure, towering and radiant like a great golden tree—he, with a heart of profound faith and devotion, joined his palms and reflected, thinking thus:
"That which all people together praise—that the Buddha is omniscient, perceives all things, and is the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha—is indeed true and not false."

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood gazing intently. When the Buddha beheld Bhadrapāla, his entire body emitted light that flowed out and illuminated him. At that moment, Bhadrapāla attained fearlessness; he circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately instruct me.

It is only now that I have attained pure faith in the Buddha; my heart yearns for the sublime Dharma and I wish to ask a question. Yet, I have long dwelt in birth and death, submerged in the suffering of afflictions with distracted and confused thoughts. Regarding the karmic actions of the precepts and so forth, I have provided no dark support through practice. Although my mind regards these matters as most profound and weighty, I do not know how to transcend this net of ignorance, delusion, and doubt within which I am caught, and thereby attain deliverance from birth and death.”

The World-Honored One is the All-Knowing One who perceives all things universally. The appearance of a Buddha is extremely rare and difficult to encounter; he is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that bestows happiness upon sentient beings.
The Buddha is a great wish-fulfilling gem, for all sentient beings derive great peace and happiness by relying upon him.
He is the great father and mother, the root of goodness for all beings; through these Buddha-parents, sentient beings are able to see the true path.
"I only pray that you will compassionately enlighten me and dispel the darkness of my doubts.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla, "Whatever you have in doubt, ask as you please."
"I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s permission, Bhadrapāla remained to one side with a focused mind, desiring to inquire further.
Then, the Elder Ānanda, seeing that the youth Bhadrapāla possessed a radiant countenance and was endowed with all auspicious marks, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is unprecedented!
This youth Bhadrapāla possesses such great merit that his radiance and complexion are so magnificent that the majestic appearances of all kings are eclipsed and do not manifest.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This noble youth Bhadrapāla, through the power of his meritorious karma, though dwelling among humans, enjoys the superior fruits of the heavens; he is peaceful, at ease, and delights in pleasure and play, his heart fully satisfied and joyful, just like Śakra."
"In Jambudvīpa, there is none who can compare with the youth Candraprabha, except perhaps for the youth Candraruci.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As for the karmic fruition, resources, and roots of goodness planted in past lives by the youth Bhadrapāla, I pray that you will speak of them for us."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Bhadrapāla currently enjoys vast resources as the fruition of his merit, as well as the excellence of his past causes; you should now listen, Ānanda.”

This youth Bhadrapāla was followed and served by sixty thousand merchant leaders whose wealth was vast and who possessed abundant stores of gold and jewels; they respectfully received his instructions. He provided sixty thousand couches furnished with bedding, woolen rugs, silken brocades, and pillows, all brilliantly colored and exquisitely adorned. These were draped with curtains of *kaurava* and *kauśeya* silk, as well as fire-resistant fabrics (*agnisparśa*) and Chinese *aṃśuka* silks, spread all around and interspersed with various precious carvings, shimmering and interlacing like a painted masterpiece.

Sixty thousand courtesans followed as attendants, their garments of *aṃśuka* silk intermingled in various colors, adorned with necklaces of gold and jewels, and dressed in fresh, brilliant, and exquisite finery that dazzled the eyes. Their touch was fine and soft like celestial *kācalindika* cloth; lightness and weight were adjusted at will to suit one’s disposition. They entertained one another with playful expressions, laughter, conversation, and song. Dignified, graceful, pure, gentle, and respectful, they served their lord; toward others, they were utterly devoid of desire. With modesty, they lowered their heads or veiled them as a mark of decorum. Their skin was even, full, soft, and smooth; the bones, veins, ankles, and joints of their hands, feet, and limbs were all entirely unvisible. Their teeth were white, even, and closely set; their hair was deep blue-black and curled to the right. They appeared as if carved from wax or painted by a master artist. Of noble lineage and illustrious reputation, their fame spread far and wide—such were the women who served him.

Furthermore, there were sixty thousand women who provided food, serving rice, cakes, and various other items in diverse colors, with fragrances and flavors as exquisite as celestial delicacies. These drinks possessed the eight virtues and brought joy to the mind upon sight; they soothed the body and pleased the heart, ripening without effort. This food of merit arrived in accordance with one's wishes, cleansing impurities and removing all ailments and evils.

The courtyards, halls, terraces, and towers numbered sixty thousand in full; they were draped and adorned with mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and various rare treasures. Interspersed with various gems, they were arranged in rows of exquisite beauty, hung with fine silks and tassels from which bells dangled. As the wind blew, they swayed and produced a harmonious, resonant chime. The ground was like lapis lazuli, reflecting myriad images; scattered flowers provided coolness and joy, where one might roam and dwell, the heart delighted and the will satisfied.

Furthermore, there were slender-waisted *bhaṇḍas*, lutes, long flutes, bronze cymbals, and pure songs; such musical sounds numbered sixty thousand in total. Their beautiful tones were harmonious, mellow, and resonant, heard from afar; as they played together in a tumultuous clamor that shook the surrounding regions, joy never ceased, brought about by the power of their meritorious deeds.

Doves and various other birds flew about and gathered there, their diverse songs blending harmoniously to delight the heart and please the ear; climbing vines and clusters of flowers entwined around the pavilions, their fresh blossoms standing out in exquisite beauty, lush and radiant. The sound of bells and musical instruments resonated like that of a celestial palace, while the corridors were as bright as the caves of Mount Sumeru illuminated by divine elixirs.

There were sixty thousand cities with high walls standing tall and watchtowers fully equipped; streets were laid out in four-way and three-way intersections, overflowing with beauty as people from all quarters gathered there. They wore various garments and spoke various languages; their laws and systems differed in ten thousand ways, and their appearances were diverse and strange. Wondrous goods were displayed in the marketplaces, and hundreds of thousands of merchant caravans thronged there; the clamor of trade resounded through the city, shaking its very precincts. The gardens were lush and verdant, with large and small trees, climbing vines, medicinal herbs, and myriad flowers blooming in competition. Clear waters encircled them, reflecting light in a variegated brilliance as bright as spread brocade. Elephants, horses, and chariots numbered in the hundreds of thousands, passing back and forth without ceasing, filling the towns and cities.

“Ānanda! The eminent and virtuous persons within the sixty thousand cities, along with the wealthy elites and the merchant lords, praised the youth Bhadrapāla day after day, proclaiming his fame and virtue, and paid him homage with reverent palms joined in worship.”
King Prasenajit of the Kingdom of Kośala possessed great wealth and prosperity through the power of his merit; yet compared to Bhadrapāla, he appeared poor and lowly.

The youth Candraprabha was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of countless female attendants who served him with reverence; he was the locus of all delights, such as affectionate play and joyful amusement, such that even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, could not equal Candraprabha by even a hundred-thousand-million-fold margin.
Bhadrapāla, though a youth of noble countenance, abundant beauty, great wealth, sovereignty, peace, and happiness, is not even a hundred thousand million times his equal to Candraprabha;
all of these are the result of past merit and cannot be achieved through mere effort.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, the youth Bhadrapāla possesses a celestial wish-fulfilling jeweled chariot, exquisitely carved and adorned with divine jewels, its radiance brilliant and dazzling. It is fashioned from celestial gold, diamond, and radiant jade, inlaid and interspersed with various precious gems so that it is as beautiful as gazing upon the stars. Its movement is as swift as the wind or the flight of a garuḍa. Riding this jeweled chariot, he reaches any jewel-island or desired destination at will, returning without physical fatigue and full of playful joy.”
At that time, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to him:

“What roots of goodness has the youth Bhadrapāla planted, and what meritorious deeds has he cultivated, such that his assets are so vast, his enjoyment of great bliss is so profound, and his palaces are so exquisite and his precious chariots so extraordinary?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because the youth Bhadrapāla previously cultivated and planted meritorious deeds within the Buddha-dharma, he has now obtained this vast reward of happiness."
In the past, there was a Buddha named Sukhābhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Bhadrapāla, at that time he left the household life within that Buddha-dharma and became a bhikṣu named Dharmacūḍa. Although his conduct regarding the precepts was deficient, he was skilled in expounding the Sūtras, Abhidharma, and Vinaya; he thoroughly mastered all the profound teachings of the Tripiṭaka and constantly proclaimed and expounded them for the sake of sentient beings. His giving of the Dharma was unceasing, and his voice was beautiful, deep, and resonant. With a straightforward and lofty tone, he analyzed and elucidated with clarity and discernment. Those who heard him were filled with joy; upon hearing the Dharma he taught, they contemplated and practiced it, and those who were liberated from the evil realms were immeasurable in number.
“Ānanda! By the merit of his Dharma-giving, the bhikṣu Dharmacaitya received the retribution of gods and humans for ninety kalpas.

Furthermore, seeing bhikṣus who maintained pure precepts yet were physically emaciated and frail, he constantly gave them food, drink, sandals, and other necessities. Because he practiced giving with such profound sincerity and a pure heart, he has now obtained this great reward of wealth and happiness, including magnificent palaces and extraordinary jeweled carriages.”
Furthermore, he encountered the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, who instructed and exhorted him, saying:
"In the future, at the place of Śākyamuni Buddha, you shall receive a prophecy of your attainment."
"Therefore, seeing me now, I have taught him the Dharma to bring him to maturity.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Bhadrapāla, this supreme youth possesses such abundant wealth, gold, and jewels, and enjoys such great power and sovereignty, yet he remains humble, gentle, and lowly, free from any sense of pride or arrogance; this is truly most extraordinary.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"One of great wisdom does not give rise to arrogance through wealth, treasures, or sensual pleasures. Bhadrapāla has long cultivated wholesome conduct; sustained by the wholesome Dharma, he constantly partakes of the fruits of merit."
Having been thus praised by the Buddha and Ānanda together, Bhadrapāla joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Out of compassion, you have gathered and protected all sentient beings; I wish to ask a few questions, so I pray that you will grant me your permission to hear them.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla, “I first grant you my leave. Whatever doubts you may have, you may now ask as you please, and I shall analyze and explain them for you.”
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Although sentient beings know that consciousness exists, it is like a treasure locked within a casket—unmanifested and unknown."
World-Honored One!
I do not know what shape this consciousness takes,
nor for what reason it is called "consciousness."

When sentient beings die, their hands and feet twitch convulsively; the color of their eyes changes, and they lose all self-control. Their sense faculties perish and the primary elements fall apart; as consciousness migrates from the body, where does it go?
What is its intrinsic nature?
What are its characteristics and forms?
How does one abandon this body and receive another body?

"How is it, World-Honored One, that while the physical constituents are discarded here, they draw along the sense bases to obtain retribution in the future, receiving various distinct and differing bodies?"
How is it that after a sentient being’s body has perished, they are again born with the various sense bases?
How is it that merit-accumulating karma performed in this life is obtained in a future life?
How is it that the body of this life performs meritorious deeds, while the body of a future life experiences their fruit?
"How does consciousness cause the body to grow?
How does consciousness enter and undergo transformation in accordance with the body?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhadrapāla! Excellent!”
Excellent question!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well!
I shall speak for your sake.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We shall do as you command.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

"The movement of consciousness, its transition, cessation, coming, and going, is like the element of wind: it is without color, without form, and cannot be manifested; yet it can set all things in motion, displaying various manifestations to the multitude. Sometimes it shakes and vibrates the forests, breaking and shattering them to produce great sounds; sometimes it becomes cold or hot, touching the bodies of sentient beings to create suffering or joy. Wind has no hands, feet, face, or features, nor does it possess any colors such as black, white, yellow, or red."
"O Bhadrapāla!
The element of consciousness is likewise: it is without color, without form, and without luminous manifestation; yet, by way of causes and conditions, it displays various distinct functions."

You should know that the dharma-realm of sensation and perception is likewise so: it is without color and without form, yet its functional efficacy is manifested through causes and conditions. O Bhadrapāla!

When sentient beings die here, the dharma-realm of sensation and perception and the consciousness-realm all depart from the body. It is consciousness that carries the dharma-realm of sensation and perception to receive another body. This is like the great element of wind blowing upon various exquisite flowers; while the flowers remain here, their fragrance flows to distant places. The substance of the wind does not grasp the fragrance of the exquisite flowers, and the substance of the fragrance, the substance of the wind, and the sense organ of the body are all devoid of form and color; yet, were it not for the power of the wind, the fragrance would not reach afar.

“Bhadrapāla! When the body of a sentient being dies, consciousness maintains the realm of sensation and cognition and proceeds to another birth. By means of the conditions of the father and mother, consciousness takes up residence therein; that the realm of sensation and cognition all follows along with consciousness is likewise so.”
Just as the nose has the power of smelling derived from the excellence of the flower, and one perceives the object of fragrance through the excellence of that smelling;
and just as the tactile quality of wind is obtained from the excellence of the body's faculty of wind, and by the power of that wind, the fragrance reaches a distance.

"In this way, from consciousness there arises sensation; from sensation there arises perception; from perception there arise mental phenomena, whereby one is ultimately able to discern what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. O Bhadrapāla!"

Furthermore, it is like a painter preparing a wall or panel; wherever he paints, he does so according to the proper method with precision and cleanliness, creating various images as he pleases. Yet, the artisan’s consciousness and intellect possess no form or color themselves, even as they produce all manner of wondrous appearances and diverse forms.
In this way, consciousness and wisdom are formless yet give rise to the six types of sensory objects: namely, because one sees forms with the eye, the eye-consciousness is formless;
because one hears sounds with the ear, sound has no form or color;
because one perceives odors with the nose, odor has no form or color; [and so forth for the remaining senses].
One knows taste through the tongue, yet taste has no form or color;
one knows touch through the body, yet touch has no form or color;
when the dharmas enter their respective objects, they are all entirely without form.
Consciousness is likewise formless. "Bhadrapāla!

When consciousness abandons this body and receives another birth, at the time of death, the consciousness of sentient beings is enveloped by the obstruction of karma; when their retribution is exhausted and life ends, it is like the consciousness of an Arhat in the meditative attainment of cessation. Just as when an Arhat enters the attainment of cessation, that Arhat’s consciousness ceases and shifts from the body."
When one dies in this manner, the consciousness abandons the body and the elements, yet by the power of mindfulness it acts thus, knowing itself as follows:
"I am so-and-so. All the deeds performed throughout one's life appear clearly in memory at the moment of death, while the body and mind are both oppressed by dual sensations.
“Bhadrapāla! What is the meaning of ‘consciousness’?
Is consciousness called a seed?”

It can produce the sprouts of the various types of retribution bodies; perception, cognition, and conceptualization are all encompassed within consciousness. Because it knows suffering and pleasure, knows evil and good, as well as the objects of both good and evil, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
As you have asked:
"How does consciousness depart from this body and receive further retribution? O Bhadrapāla!
The transference of consciousness to a body is like the reflection of a face appearing in a mirror, or like the impression of a seal manifesting upon clay.

It is like the rising of the sun: wherever its light reaches, all darkness is dispelled; when the sun sets and its light fades, the darkness returns as before. Darkness has no substance or form; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet it occupies its place. Consciousness is likewise:
it has no substance and no form, but it manifests through sensation and perception.

Consciousness resides within the body like the essence of darkness; it cannot be seen when looked upon, nor can it be grasped. It is like a mother carrying a child in her womb, who cannot know for herself whether it is male or female, black, white, or yellow, whether its faculties are complete or incomplete, or whether its hands, feet, ears, and eyes are normal or abnormal. When the child moves due to the heat of food or drink, it perceives pain; likewise, when sentient beings come and go, bend and stretch, blink their eyes, speak, laugh, converse, carry loads, bear heavy weights, or perform various tasks, the characteristics of consciousness are fully manifest, yet they cannot know where this consciousness is located, nor do they know its form while it dwells within the body.

“Bhadrapāla! The self-nature of consciousness pervades all sense bases (*āyatana*), yet it is not defiled by those sense bases. Consciousness dwells throughout the six faculties, the six objects, and the five aggregates of affliction (*kleśa-skandha*) without being stained by them; it is through this that the functional activity of consciousness is revealed.”
“Bhadrapāla! It is like a wooden mechanical device that, when attached to a single point, performs various actions—whether walking, leaping, jumping, or dancing.
What do you think?”
"By whose power is that which is produced by a mechanical device accomplished?
Bhadrapāla said to the Buddha, "My wisdom is narrow and shallow; I am not able to resolve this."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "You should know that all this is the power of the karma one creates. Created karma has no form; it is merely the movement of consciousness!

Thus, the mechanism of the body performs all its various activities through the power of consciousness. Whether it be the supernatural powers of sages, gandharvas, nāgas, spirits, humans, devas, asuras, or the karmic actions of various realms—all depend entirely upon it. Consciousness can produce the body just as a craftsman operates a mechanical device. Consciousness has no physical form, yet it universally sustains the Dharma-realm, is fully endowed with the power of wisdom, and can even know the events of past lives."
For example, just as the light of the sun shines equally upon sentient beings of evil karma and upon impure corpses and stinking filth without partiality, and is not defiled by those evils;
so too is consciousness: although it dwells within the bodies of the various evil destinies—such as those of pigs and dogs that consume impurities—it is not defiled by them.
“Bhadrapāla! When consciousness abandons this body, it migrates according to its wholesome or unwholesome karma to receive further retribution.

It is like the element of wind that emerges from deep mountains and remote valleys; if it enters a grove of *campaka* trees filled with various fragrances, the wind becomes fragrant. If it passes through places of filth, corpses, stench, and impurity, the wind becomes foul. If the wind encounters both fragrance and stench together, the wind will possess both fragrance and stench simultaneously, though whichever is more intense manifests first. Wind has no physical form, and fragrance and stench have no physical form; yet, the wind carries fragrance and stench and transfers them to distant places.”

When consciousness abandons this body and migrates to receive further retribution according to its wholesome and unwholesome karma, it is likewise like that element of wind carrying the fragrance or stench of objects to another place.

Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream who sees various forms and engages in diverse activities, yet remains unaware that they are lying in peaceful sleep; when a person of merit reaches the end of life and their consciousness migrates, it is likewise peaceful and unconscious. This transition occurs as calmly as a dream, without any fear. The departure of the consciousness does not occur through the throat, the mouth, or any of the bodily apertures; its point of origin cannot be measured, nor can its path or exit be known.
At that time, the youth Bhadrapāla, the Supreme One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the eggs of chickens, geese, and the like have not yet matured, and their shells are completely fine and dense, through what opening does consciousness enter?”
“The child dies within the egg; the shell is not broken, nor is there any fissure or aperture.
From where does consciousness emerge? The Buddha said, “Bhadrapāla!”

For example, when black sesame seeds are perfumed with *campaka* flowers, the oil produced is fragrant and delicious, known as *campaka* oil; it differs from ordinary sesame oil in quality as they are worlds apart. Originally the oil had no fragrance, but because the seeds were perfumed with flowers, the oil subsequently became fragrant. This fragrance does not break through the sesame to enter, nor does it break through the sesame to exit; furthermore, it has no physical substance that remains within the oil. Rather, by the power of causes and conditions, the fragrance migrates into the oil, and the oil becomes a fragrant essence.
The entry and exit of the consciousness of a chicken or duck embryo into its egg is also like this.
Just as the fragrance of *campaka* flowers migrates into oil, the migration of consciousness is like the sun’s radiance, the luster of a mani-jewel, or fire produced from wood.

Furthermore, it is like a seed planted in the earth: its substance transforms within the soil, while sprouts, stalks, and leaves manifest fully on the outside; it produces various flowers of white, non-white, red, and other colors, which ripen with diverse powers and flavors, resulting in various distinctions. Although they all equally rely upon the great earth and the four elements for their sustenance, each differs according to the specific seed from which it arises. In this same way, the single consciousness of the dharma-realm gives rise to all bodies within the cycle of birth and death—whether black, white, yellow, or red—and manifests in various distinct categories, such as those who are gentle and harmonious or those who are wrathful and violent.

“Bhadrapāla! Consciousness has no hands or feet, nor does it have limbs or speech. Because the power of mindfulness within the *dharmadhātu* is so great, when sentient beings die, consciousness abandons this body. Consciousness and the power of mindfulness together serve as the seed for future births; yet one cannot obtain the *dharmadhātu* apart from consciousness, nor can one obtain consciousness apart from the *dharmadhātu*.
"Consciousness migrates in conjunction with the subtle element of wind, the sphere of perception, the sphere of feeling, and the sphere of mental phenomena.
Bhadrapāla said to the Buddha,
"If this is so, World-Honored One, why do you say that consciousness is formless?"
The Buddha said, “Bhadrapāla,
there are two kinds of form:”
First, the internal; second, the external.
The internal refers to visual consciousness, while the eye is the external.
Likewise, auditory consciousness is internal, while the ear is external.
The nose-consciousness is internal, while the nose is external;
the tongue-consciousness is internal, while the tongue is external;
the body-consciousness is internal, while the body is external.

“Bhadrapāla! It is like a man born blind who, in a dream, sees beautiful forms—hands, feet, face, and features all exquisite and lovely—and consequently gives rise to great love and delight within the dream. Upon waking, however, he sees nothing at all. When the night has ended and it is bright with day, and a great crowd has gathered, the blind man then recounts the pleasures of his dream: ‘I saw a beautiful woman whose appearance was peerless; there were flourishing gardens and groves, and hundreds of thousands of people, adorned and sporting together. Her skin was radiant and lustrous, her shoulders were firm and full, and her arms were long and rounded like an elephant’s trunk. In my dream, I obtained great happiness, and my heart was filled with joy and admiration.’”
“Bhadrapāla! This person has been blind since birth and has never seen objects; how could they see forms within a dream?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Please grant us an exposition.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

“That which is seen within a dream is called the domain of the internal eye; it is a discernment of wisdom and not something seen by the physical eye. As for this domain of the internal eye, by the power of mindfulness, it appears momentarily even to the blind in their dreams.”
Furthermore, by the power of mindfulness, one awakens and recollects it;
the internal form perceived by consciousness is likewise so. "Moreover, Bhadrapāla!"

When the body dies and consciousness migrates, it is like a seed cast into the earth: sustained by the four great elements, the sprout, stem, branches, and leaves gradually transform and develop. Consciousness, sustained by the four dharmas of mindfulness, sensation, the wholesome, and the unwholesome, likewise abandons the body and migrates in this same manner.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do wholesome and unwholesome dharmas sustain consciousness?”
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

“For example, suppose there is a wondrous crystal gem; depending on whether the object it rests upon is black or white, the color of the gem becomes white or black accordingly. It is the same with consciousness being sustained by wholesome or unwholesome dharmas: depending on what sustains it, it becomes wholesome or unwholesome, and thus undergoes transformation and receives retribution.”
Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does this body receive consciousness?
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:

"This consciousness has no accumulation, no aggregation, and no growth. For example, when a sprout arises, it does not arise from a seed that remains unchanged, nor does it arise from a seed that has been destroyed; yet, at the moment the sprout arises, the seed undergoes transformation and destruction."
"Bhadrapāla! What do you think?
Where does that sprout abide? Where does it reside?"
Is it the seed?
Is it the branch?
Or is it the stem, the trunk, or the leaves?
"Did he stop in the tree?
Bhadrapāla replied to the Buddha, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The sprout has no place of rest. “It is so, Bhadrapāla!”

Consciousness within the body has no fixed location; it is not the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, or body. When the sprout arises from the seed, consciousness is like a subtle awareness; up until the union of the flower, consciousness is as if possessing sensation (*vedanā*); from the opening of the bud and the blooming of the flower until the formation of the fruit, consciousness is as if possessing a body. As consciousness gives rise to the body, it pervades all its limbs and members, yet if one seeks the place where consciousness dwells, its location cannot be found.

If one excludes the body of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*), it will not arise; just as when a tree’s fruit ripens, it is fit to serve as the seed for a future tree, whereas that which has not ripened is not, so too, when the retribution-body dies and the fruit has ripened, the seed of consciousness manifests. With consciousness as cause, there is sensation (*vedanā*); with sensation as cause, there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Bound by attachment to craving, one gives rise to mental attention (*manasikāra*). Consciousness grasps this attention and, according to wholesome or unwholesome karma, together with the wind-element (*vāyudhātu*), it becomes aware of the parents. When the conditions and causes coincide, consciousness then takes up residence therein, just as a person’s facial reflection appears in a mirror. If the face is neither clean nor bright, the image does not appear; only when the mirror is clear and the face is present does the reflection manifest. The image within the mirror has no sensation and no mental attention, yet it follows the person’s movements—bending and stretching, looking down and up, opening the mouth to speak or jest, walking, coming, advancing, and stopping—in all its various activities.
“Bhadrapāla!
By whose power does this reflection appear?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The power of this person arises because there is a face; thus there is a reflection of the face. The color of the reflection is like the color of the face, and whether the sense organs are complete or incomplete, they are all exactly like those of the face."
The Buddha said:
"The face is the cause of the reflection, and the mirror is the condition for the reflection; through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, the reflection appears.

Likewise, by virtue of consciousness as the cause, there arise feeling, perception, mental formations, and all mental factors; with the parents as the condition, through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, the body appears."

Just as with that body and mirror—when the body moves away, the reflection in the mirror vanishes; yet the body retains the image, which may appear separately within water or other media—so too it is when consciousness abandons this body:
carrying its good and evil karma, it migrates to receive further retribution.

Furthermore, it is like the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and other such trees: although their seeds are small, they are able to produce great trees; the tree, in turn, produces seeds. Once the seeds have abandoned the old tree, they give rise to a new tree. Thus, after a long time, the substance and strength of the old tree decline, its sap and juices are exhausted, and it withers, dries up, and rots away.
In this way, when the consciousness of these various small living beings abandons the body, it rides upon its own karma and may receive various kinds of large bodies.
Furthermore, just as various seeds—such as barley, wheat, sesame, mung beans, and mocha—sprout, grow stems, flowers, and fruits, and reach maturity because they possess the seed;

so too, because consciousness exists, the migrating class of beings immediately possesses sensation (*vedanā*). From sensation comes feeling (*vedanā*), which maintains good and evil karma and leads to the reception of various bodies.

Furthermore, it is like a bee that rests upon a flower, delighting in and becoming attached to it; it sucks the nectar of the flower to nourish itself. The bee abandons this flower to dwell upon another; it may leave a fragrant one for a foul-smelling one, or leave a foul-smelling one for a fragrant one. Wherever it goes, there is no place where it does not feel self-love, attachment, and greedy clinging.

Consciousness is also like this: by means of meritorious karma, it obtains a celestial body and experiences the fruit of supreme bliss; or, discarding the celestial body, by means of evil karma, it receives the retribution of hell and experiences the fruit of manifold suffering. As it transmigrates through the cycle of existence, it becomes various kinds of bodies. Consciousness is like saffron, red-blue (indigo), or white lotus (puṇḍarīka): their seeds are all white. If one breaks open a seed, no sprout, flower, or different color is seen within it. Yet, when planted in the earth and moistened with water, there are then sprouts and so forth; they grow according to the seasons until flowers and fruits flourish, appearing in various colors such as red or white. These colors and the sprouts do not exist within the seed, yet apart from the seed, they cannot arise at all.

Once consciousness has abandoned the body, it no longer perceives within that consciousness the causal conditions for the union of the physical form, features, sense faculties, and sense bases. Consciousness, through its subtle seeing and subtle hearing, as well as its engagement with sounds, touches, tastes, mental objects (*dharma*), and thoughts, recognizes the wholesome and unwholesome karma it has created and thereby takes on a bodily retribution. Just as a silkworm makes a cocoon, binding itself by its own making, and undergoes transformation therein; so too is consciousness: consciousness itself produces a body and then envelops itself within it.

Having abandoned this body, it receives further retribution; because there is a seed, there is form, odor, taste, and touch. As consciousness abandons the body and migrates according to its destination, all the sense faculties, their objects, sensations, and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) follow after it.
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem follows wherever it goes and all objects of enjoyment follow it, and just as light follows wherever the sun is;
so too is consciousness: wherever it migrates, sensation, perception, volition, and the dharma-realm all follow it.

Consciousness abandons the body while encompassing all natures; with form as its cause for the body, it is a body without bone or flesh. Because it possesses the various sense faculties (*indriya*), there is sensation (*vedanā*), sublime mindfulness, and the cognition that grasps good and evil. This is like the various fruits of the jujube, pomegranate, mango (*āmra*), wood-apple (*bilva*), *nīla*, *kapittha*, and *kapiṭha*, which may be pungent, bitter, sour, sweet, salty, or astringent. Their flavors and potencies differ individually; their contributions to digestion and maturation are not uniform. Once the fruit has decayed, the flavor and potency follow the seed in migrating and transforming to arise again.

Thus, as this seed of consciousness migrates according to its conditions, sensation, mindfulness, and both good and evil all follow it; because one knows that this body is abandoned and another retribution-body is received, it is called consciousness;

because one knows good and evil karma and knows that karma follows oneself, and knows that one maintains the karma through migration and transformation to receive retribution, it is called consciousness;
because one fully knows all that the body does, it is called consciousness.

For example, the element of wind has no form that can be grasped and no substance that can be held; yet, through causes and conditions, it performs various functions that manifest the existence of the element of wind: it sustains cold and heat, carries fragrance and stench, shakes and vibrates the forest trees, or fans and strikes them down. In this same way, consciousness has no form or substance and cannot be apprehended by sight or hearing;

yet, through causes and conditions, the characteristics of consciousness are fully manifested. By means of consciousness, the body is sustained; the body experiences pleasure and pain, its complexion becomes full and radiant, and its movements—coming and going, advancing and stopping—as well as its speech, laughter, joy, sorrow, and various activities become clearly evident. Thus, one should know that consciousness exists.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara at the Eastern Taiyuan Temple in the first year of the Yonglong era of the Great Tang dynasty; included in the *Dazhou Catalogue*.
*Mahāyāna-vijñapti-prakāśana-sūtra*, Scroll One;
*Mahāyāna-vijñapti-prakāśana-sūtra*, Scroll Two.

At that time, in the assembly, there was the youth Candradhvajasamudgata who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: Translated by the Śramaṇa Divākara of the kingdom of Central India, by imperial decree. At that time, in the assembly, there was the youth Candradhvajasamudgata, who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is the cause of the perception of form seen?
How is the cause of desire seen?”
"What is the cause for the view of views?
What is the cause for the clinging to precepts and rituals?
The Buddha told Candraprabha:

"The wise perceive the realm of wisdom, while the foolish perceive the realm of folly. When the wise behold various beautiful and lovely forms, they understand them to be foul and loathsome—merely lumps of flesh, sinews, bones, pus, and blood; large and small vessels, large and small intestines; lymph, marrow, membranes, kidneys, heart, spleen, gallbladder, liver, lungs, stomach, and the raw and cooked viscera; yellow phlegm, mucus, saliva, hair, beard, body hair, and nails; excrement and urine, all wrapped in thin skin, impure, filthy, exposed, fearsome, and detestable. Indeed, all forms arise from the four great elements; these are the causes of form."

“Candraprabha! Just as the physical body is produced by one’s parents: the solidity of the body is the earth element; its moisture and fluidity is the water element; its warmth and maturation is the fire element; its movement and fluctuation is the wind element; and whatever is perceived through cognition, including the spheres of thought, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch—all these constitute consciousness.”
The youth Candravrata again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
At the time of death, how does consciousness depart from the body?"
"How does consciousness migrate to the body?
How does consciousness know that it is now abandoning this body?
The Buddha told Candraprabha:

“Sentient beings receive retribution according to their karma; the stream of consciousness continues in succession, sustaining the body without interruption. When the allotted period ends and the retribution is exhausted, consciousness abandons the body and migrates to receive another existence according to its karma.”
For example, when water and milk are mixed and boiled by the power of heat, the milk, the water, and the cream each separate.
In this same way, Moon-Real!

when the life of sentient beings ends, they are dispersed by the power of karma; the physical form, consciousness, and the various sense bases and elements each disperse. Consciousness, as its support, takes up the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), mindfulness of the realm of phenomena, and both wholesome and unwholesome karma, migrating to receive another retribution.

"Candraprabha! It is just as, for example, when the great *mahā-sugandhika* ghee is prepared by blending various medicinal herbs through the power of their flavors and the process of refinement, it becomes this great *mahā-sugandhika* ghee. It abandons the nature of ordinary ghee and maintains the power of the medicinal herbs; its six tastes—bitter, pungent, sour, salty, astringent, and sweet—sustain the human body and provide it with color, fragrance, and flavor.
In the same way, when consciousness abandons this body, it carries away wholesome and unwholesome karma, as well as the *dharmadhātu* and so forth, migrating to receive further retribution."

“Candraprabha! Just as ghee is the body of medicinal substances, when various medicines are combined they form what is greatly auspicious; likewise, when various dharmas and faculties are combined they form karma. Just as the tastes and textures of various medicines contribute to the formation of ghee, so too does karma contribute to consciousness. When one consumes this greatly auspicious ghee, it becomes radiant, full, beautiful in complexion, peaceful, and free from affliction—just as when consciousness is supported by wholesome [karma], one obtains various pleasant retributions.

If one consumes ghee in a manner contrary to the Dharma, the countenance changes for the worse, becoming haggard, bloodless, deathly pale, and ashen—just as when consciousness is supported by unwholesome [karma], one obtains various painful retributions.”
“Candraprabha! Just as precious ghee, though lacking hands, feet, or eyes, can take up excellent medicines with their color, fragrance, taste, and potency;

so too does consciousness: it takes up the dharmadhātu, sensations, and various wholesome karmas, abandons this physical body, and receives a divine, wondrous mindfulness within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). It beholds the six heavens of desire and the sixteen hells, and seeing its own body—its hands and feet dignified and its sense faculties beautiful—it looks upon the discarded corpse and says:”
"This was my body in a previous life.

Furthermore, he saw celestial palaces of sublime and wondrous appearance, adorned with various ornaments, covered by flowers, fruits, shrubs, trees, and climbing vines, their radiance brilliant and magnificent like freshly refined gold inlaid with myriad jewels.

Having seen this, his mind is filled with great joy; due to that great joy and love, consciousness then entrusts itself to it. This person of wholesome karma, when casting off one body and taking up another, experiences peace and happiness without suffering, like a rider who abandons one horse to mount another.

It is just as when a powerful warrior, fully equipped with martial skill and strategy, sees the enemy forces approaching; he dons sturdy armor and mounts a swift steed, proceeding without fear. Likewise, one who relies on the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) abandons inhalation and exhalation, relinquishes the body of the sense-spheres (*āyatana*), and migrates to receive superior bliss, being reborn therein from the Brahma-world up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
At that time, the Prince Mahauṣadha rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When consciousness departs from the body, what form or appearance does it take?”
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
What you have now asked concerns the most profound realm of the Buddhas; apart from the Tathāgata, there is no one else capable of understanding it.
Thereupon, the youth Bhadrapāla-uttara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The questions posed by Prince Mahauṣadha are profound; his wisdom is subtle, keen, and decisive.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

“This Prince Mahauṣadha has already planted roots of goodness under the Buddha Vipaśyin. In five hundred previous lives, he was born into the families of non-Buddhist practitioners; while serving as a non-Buddhist practitioner, he constantly contemplated the meaning of consciousness.”
What is consciousness? What constitutes consciousness?
For five hundred lifetimes I have been unable to discern it; I know nothing of the origins or the course of consciousness as it departs and returns.
"Today, for the sake of shattering the net of doubt and enabling its resolution, I shall do so.
Thereupon, the youth Bhadrapāla-uttara addressed Prince Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Excellent!"

Excellent! What you have now asked is subtle and profoundly deep. The inquiry of Candravatī is shallow and narrow, like that of an infant whose mind wanders toward external objects while remaining ignorant of the internal. The True Dharma is rarely heard and the Buddhas are difficult to encounter; the Buddha’s perfect and vast wisdom, his unfathomable profound insight, and the most wondrous principles should be sought through dedicated and earnest petition.

At that time, Prince Mahauṣadha, seeing the Buddha’s countenance radiant and joyful like an autumn lotus in full bloom, leaped for joy with great delight; with his palms joined in single-minded devotion, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I cherish the profound Dharma and thirst for the profound Dharma; I constantly fear that the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa before I have heard the True Dharma. Among the sentient beings of the five turbidities, they are ignorant and know nothing, failing to distinguish between good and evil. Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome, or what is matured and immature, they lack awakening and understanding, remaining deluded as they revolve through the miserable realms of birth and death.
The Buddha told Prince Mahābhaiṣajya:

“The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter and difficult to obtain. In the past, for the sake of even half a verse, I climbed a mountain and threw myself down, relinquishing my life; for the sake of seeking the True Dharma, I underwent immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of various hardships.”
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Whatever you desire to ask, ask freely; I shall explain it to you in detail.
Prince Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, we shall follow your instructions,
World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of consciousness?”
"I pray that you will grant me an exposition.
The Buddha told Mahābhaiṣajya:

"It is like a person's reflection appearing in water; this image cannot be grasped, it cannot be distinguished as either existent or non-existent, like the form of a *kuraṅga* deer, or like the image of a thirsty craving."
The Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is craving?”
The Buddha said:
"It is like a person facing a pleasing form; when the eye faculty moves toward it, this is called craving.
It is just as when one holds a bright mirror and looks at the reflection of one's own face: if the mirror is removed, the reflection of the face is no longer seen."
The transmigration of consciousness is likewise thus: the forms of good and evil karma, as well as the images of consciousness, are all invisible.
It is just as one born blind cannot perceive the rising and setting of the sun, nor the light and darkness of day and night;
that consciousness is unable to see is also like this.

Within the body, craving, sensation, and perception are invisible; the great elements, the sense bases, and the aggregates of the body are all consciousness. All material forms—the body, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and even the immaterial mind that experiences pleasure and pain, are all likewise consciousness.

“Mahābhaiṣajya! It is like a person whose tongue, upon obtaining food, discerns the six tastes—sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and astringent; both the tongue and the food possess form and color, yet taste itself has no form. Furthermore, one perceives various sensations through the body’s bones, marrow, flesh, and blood; while the bones and so forth have form, sensation has neither form nor color. The knowledge of the fruits of merit and demerit is likewise.”
Then the youth Bhadrapāla, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can this consciousness discern merit and non-merit?”
The Buddha said: "Listen well!

It is not that one who has not yet seen the Truth can perceive consciousness. Consciousness cannot be seen; it is not like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand. Consciousness does not reside within the eyes and other sense organs. If consciousness were located within the eyes and other organs, one should be able to see consciousness by cutting them open."

Bhadrapāla! Just as the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, perceive consciousness as formless, so too do I perceive consciousness as formless. Consciousness cannot be seen by the ordinary and ignorant; it is merely revealed through metaphors.
Bhadrapāla! If you wish to know the offenses and merits of consciousness, listen now!
It is, for example, like a person who has been possessed by various devas, gandharvas, or spirits such as the skandhas.
Bhadrapāla! What do you think?
As for that which is possessed by devas and other spirits, can the essence of that possession be found and seen within the body?
Bhadrapāla said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"When one is possessed by devas or other spirits, the essence of that possession has no color and no form; whether sought within or without the body, it cannot be seen at all.
"Bhadrapāla! [the Buddha said.]

Regarding those whose merit is superior to that which is possessed by the great devas: one must provide excellent incense and flowers, burn various renowned perfumes, and arrange pure, delicious food and drink. All sacrificial implements and offerings must be exquisitely clean and pure. Thus, when this consciousness is supported by such merit, it attains the fruits of nobility and peace and happiness:

either becoming a king of men, or a high minister, or one of noble reputation and high status, or one with sovereign wealth, or a leader among many, or a great merchant chief, or even attaining a celestial body and experiencing the supreme fruits of the heavens.

Because consciousness is supported by merit, the body obtains the retribution of happiness; it is like being possessed by a powerful celestial deity who enjoys exquisite flowers, fragrances, and delicious food and drink, whereby the patient immediately becomes joyful and at ease. That one now attains nobility, wealth, and sovereignty should be understood as entirely resulting from consciousness being supported by merit, whereby the body obtains the fruit of happiness.

“Bhadrapāla! Those who are possessed by inferior and evil spirits such as the *pūtana* come to love impure things such as excrement, filth, putrefaction, mucus, and saliva; they seek relief and joy through offerings of these, and their illnesses are cured. By the power of the spirit, such a person follows the spirit’s desires and takes pleasure in impurity, stench, decay, and excrement.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) supported by sin is likewise: it may lead to rebirth in poverty, or among hungry ghosts (*preta*), or among various animals that consume filth within the manifold miserable realms (*durgati*). Through consciousness supported by sin, the body reaps the fruit of suffering.”

"Bhadrapāla! When the superior devas and heavenly beings possess a person, their bodies are without substance or form, yet they receive various kinds of fragrant and pure offerings; likewise, when consciousness possesses no form, it receives the retribution of supreme bliss for its merit.

When inferior and evil spirits such as the *pūtanas* possess someone, that person immediately receives impure and foul food and drink; likewise, consciousness, supported by its sinful karma, obtains various forms of suffering as its retribution."

"Bhadrapāla! You should know that consciousness has no physical form, just as the body possessed by devas and other spirits; and just as one obtains good or bad results from offerings and food, so too does one receive the retribution of suffering or pleasure based on the merit or demerit one has accumulated."
The Prince Mahauṣadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does one perceive the causes of desire?”
The Buddha said:
"Great Medicine!

Desire arises through mutual dependence, just as fire is produced when two pieces of wood used for kindling depend upon each other and human effort is applied. In this same way, desire arises depending upon consciousness, as well as depending upon the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects of male and female."
For example, as fruit arises from a flower, there is no fruit within the flower; when the fruit is produced, the flower perishes. In the same way, consciousness is manifested through the body:

if one seeks consciousness by following the body, consciousness cannot be seen. When the fruit of consciousness’s karma arises, the body then passes away and perishes; the impure substances such as the body’s bones and marrow all completely dissolve and disperse.
Furthermore, just as a seed carries the future fruit’s taste, color, fragrance, and texture, transplanting itself to grow;

so too is it with consciousness: when it abandons this body, it carries its wholesome and unwholesome karma—along with sensation, perception, and mental attention—to receive the retribution of a future birth.

Furthermore, it is like a man and a woman who, having met in the joy of desire, depart from one another; so too, consciousness and karma unite, bound by attachment and clinging to the savor of experience with greed and parsimony. When the retribution is exhausted and they separate, one receives retribution according to karma. Within the causal conditions of the parents, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) encounters them; through the power of karma, consciousness arises and obtains the fruit of a body. Both affectionate love and karma are devoid of form or substance, yet they mutually cause one another to arise within the realm of desire; this is the cause of desire.
"Mahābhaiṣajya! What is the view of clinging to precepts as the cause?
'Precepts' refers to the rules established by a teacher, such as the practices of not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, and not drinking intoxicants."

"Grasping" (upādāna) means clinging. This refers to the view held regarding precepts, such as thinking: "By virtue of maintaining these precepts, I shall attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin). Because of this cause, one obtains superior existence, namely, receiving the bodies of humans, devas, and so forth; all of these are tainted (sāsrava) virtues, not untainted (anāsrava) virtues.

Untainted wholesome states have no ripening fruit within the aggregates; however, this clinging to precepts and rituals is tainted and planted therein. Because one clings to the consciousness that perceives wholesome and unwholesome karma as impure, and because it is a cause of affliction, one undergoes the suffering of feverish distress. This constitutes the cause of the view of clinging to precepts and rituals.
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does consciousness take on a celestial body, and even take on the body of a hell-being?
The Buddha said:

“Mahābhaiṣajya! Consciousness and the dharma-realm sustain a subtle vision; this is not that which the physical eye relies upon as the cause for seeing. When this subtle vision unites with the realm of merit, one sees the celestial palaces and the delights of sensual play. Having seen them, one rejoices, and consciousness becomes bound and attached, forming the thought: ‘I shall go there.’”
With passionate attachment and longing as the cause for rebirth, having seen his own former body lying in the charnel ground, he thinks to himself:
"This corpse was my great spiritual friend; because of the accumulation of various wholesome karmas by him, I have now obtained this celestial retribution."
The Great Medicine said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Since this consciousness already possesses such attachment and esteem for the corpse, why does it not take up residence there?”
The Buddha said, "Great Medicine!
For example, suppose one has cut off and discarded one's hair and beard; even though they were once jet-black, lustrous, and fragrant, could they ever be planted back upon the body to grow again?"
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the Buddha, “No,
World-Honored One!”
"Once the hair and beard have been discarded, they cannot be replanted upon the body to grow again.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great Medicine!"
"Once the corpse has been discarded, consciousness can no longer be entrusted with receiving retribution.
Mahābhaiṣajya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

This consciousness is profound, obscure, and subtle; it has no substance that can be grasped and no form that can be sought. How, then, can it support sentient beings with massive bodies such as elephants?
Even if their bodies were as solid as diamond, how could it penetrate the body of a powerful man and support one whose strength rivals nine elephants?
The Buddha said, “Great Medicine!

It is like the element of wind, which has no substance and no form; though it dwells within deep valleys or narrow crevices, its emergence can be violent and fierce, even capable of toppling Mount Sumeru and grinding it into fine dust.”
“Mahauṣadhi! What are the color and appearance of the wind-mahābhūta of Mount Sumeru?
Mahauṣadhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The wind element is subtle, without substance and without form.
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!..."
The wind element is subtle and wondrous, lacking both substance and form;
consciousness is likewise subtle and formless, yet it can sustain both large and small bodies, whether receiving the body of a mosquito or the body of an elephant.
For example, like a bright lamp whose flame is subtle and refined, when placed within a room, all darkness is dispelled regardless of the room's size;
consciousness is likewise, sustaining itself according to the magnitude of its various karmic causes.
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics and nature of these various karmas?”
“By what causes and conditions does it manifest?
The Buddha said,
“Great Medicine!”
To be born in the palaces of the devas, partaking of exquisite celestial food and dwelling in peace and happiness—all this is brought about by the fruits of karma.

It is like a person wandering through a vast wilderness in parching thirst: one who finds cool, sweet water experiences relief, while another who finds nothing endures the suffering of thirst. No one brought the cool water to the first, nor was anyone obstructed from giving it to the second; each receives their retribution of pleasure or pain according to their own karmic causes.

"Mahābhaiṣajya! You should view good and evil karma in this way: like the two phases of the moon in the sky, white and black; or like a raw fruit that, through the increase of the fire element, ripens and its color changes. Likewise, because of the increase of merit, this body is born into a noble family, with abundant assets, overflowing gold and jewels, and manifest, flourishing excellence; or one is born in the palaces of the devas, enjoying happiness and sovereignty—all these are the manifestations of the auspicious signs of virtuous karma."

It is like planting a seed in the earth; the fruit appears at the top of the tree, yet that seed does not travel from branch to branch to reach the treetop. Even if one were to cut through the trunk of the tree, the seed would not be seen there; no one carries the seed up onto the branches. Once the tree has grown with firm roots, though one searches for the original seed, it is nowhere to be found. In this same way, all wholesome and unwholesome karmas depend upon the body, yet though one searches within the body, the karma itself is not seen.

Just as there are flowers because of seeds, yet there are no flowers within the seeds; and there are fruits because of flowers, yet there are no fruits within the flowers—and although the flowers and fruits develop further and further, they are not seen [as inherently existing therein]—so too it is with the body and karma:
there is a body because of karma, and there is karma because of the body; yet there is no karma within the body, nor is there a body within karma. It is exactly like this.

Just as when a flower ripens and falls, its fruit then appears; so too, when the body ripens and perishes, the karmic fruit finally emerges. Just as the causes for flowers and fruits exist within the seed, so too does the body contain the causes of wholesome and unwholesome karma. That karma has no form, nor does it possess any manifest characteristic of ripening.

Just as a human shadow has no substance and is unimpeded, cannot be grasped, and does not cling to the person, yet moves forward and backward, coming and going, in accordance with the person's movements—nor is it seen that the shadow emerges from the body;
so too is the karmic body. Where there is a body, there is karma, yet karma is not seen; it neither clings to the body, nor does it exist apart from the body while being able to produce karma.

Just as medicinal herbs with various tastes—bitter, pungent, and astringent—can cleanse and eliminate all diseases, making the body full and joyful and the complexion radiant, so that those who see them know they have taken excellent medicine; and just as the taste of the medicine can be perceived while its matured efficacy is formless, invisible to the eye and ungraspable by the hand, yet it nourishes the person’s skin and complexion;
so too is it with karma: though it has no physical substance, it is able to nourish the body.

Those supported by virtuous karma possess abundant and beautiful provisions such as food, drink, and clothing; they have well-proportioned hands and feet, a handsome appearance, and magnificent dwellings; they accumulate mani-jewels, gold, silver, and various treasures; they enjoy peace, happiness, and delightful pleasures to their heart's content—know that these are the signs of virtuous karma.

To be born among the lowly, in border regions, or in poverty; to lack basic necessities and long for the happiness of others; to have coarse and poor food, or to go without food altogether; to have a wretched appearance and dwell in a humble place—one should know that these are the signs of evil karma.

It is just as a bright mirror reflects the beauty or ugliness of a face; yet the reflected image has no substance and cannot be apprehended. In this same way, consciousness relies upon wholesome or unwholesome karma to be born among humans or devas, or to be born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and so forth.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
You should view the karma and consciousness in this way as they combine, migrate, and transform.
Mahābhaiṣajya said:
“World-Honored One!
How can such a subtle consciousness maintain the various sense organs and grasp this great body?
The Buddha said:

“Mahābhaiṣajya! It is like a hunter who enters a mountain forest carrying a bow and a poisoned arrow to shoot a fragrant elephant. Once the arrow’s poison touches its blood, the venom spreads through the elephant’s body; its limbs fail and its senses and objects of perception are simultaneously lost. As the poison flows to its vital points, the color of its body becomes blue and red, like clotted blood. Having killed the elephant, the poison then passes away.”
"What do you think?
Can the amount and size of the poison be compared to that of the elephant's body?
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The amount and size of the poison compared to the elephant’s body are so vastly different that they cannot be equated, just as Mount Sumeru compared to a mustard seed.”
“Great Medicine!
In this same way, consciousness abandons this body to take up the various sense faculties; it abandons these various elements and undergoes transformation according to karma, just so.”
The Great Medicine again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How is it that the subtle consciousness sustains this vast body without becoming weary?"
The Buddha said, "Mahābhaiṣajya!

Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas high. The two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, each circle it three times; when these two nāgas breathe heavily, they cause Mount Sumeru to tremble and shake, and all the water within the inner ocean is transformed into poison."
These two nāga kings are long, powerful, and strong; the two great nāga kings, Vāsuki and Takṣaka, are also equal to them.
What do you think?
“Is there any difference between the consciousness of the four dragon kings and the consciousness of mosquitoes and gnats?
Great Medicine replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"The consciousness of the four dragons and that of a mosquito or gnat are no different. "Great Medicine!
It is like a single small drop of *vatsanābha* poison entering the mouths of the four dragons, whereby the four dragons would immediately die."
"What do you think?
Between a small drop of medicinal poison and the poison from the mouth of a nāga, which poison is greater?
Great Medicine replied to the Buddha:
“The venom from a dragon’s mouth is great, while the poison of a small drop of medicine is extremely slight. “Great Medicine!

A sentient being with a massive body has a strength equal to nine elephants, yet the subtle consciousness is without color and without form; it cannot be measured by discrimination, and its maintenance according to karma is likewise so.”
Suppose there were a *nyagrodha* seed, extremely minute; yet when planted, it gives rise to a tree so vast and luxuriant that its branches and twigs number in the hundreds of thousands.
What do you think?
Is the seed and the tree similar in size?
Mahābhaiṣajya said:
“World-Honored One!
The disparity between that seed and the tree is like comparing the hole of a lotus fiber to the realm of empty space.”
“In this way, Great Medicine!
One cannot find the tree within the seed; yet, were it not for the seed, the tree would not arise.

A minute nyagrodha seed can produce a great tree, and subtle consciousness can produce a great body. Within consciousness, one cannot find the body, yet apart from consciousness, the body does not exist.”
The Great Medicine further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can consciousness—which is adamantine, firm, and indestructible—dwell within this body that is precarious, fragile, and subject to rapid decay?
The Buddha said:

"Mahābhaiṣajya! It is like a poor man who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). By the power of that jewel, there appear high halls with carved ornamentation, exquisite and beautiful palaces, lush gardens and groves, flourishing flowers and fruits, elephants, horses, and female attendants; all necessities and articles of enjoyment arrive spontaneously.

Later, when that person loses the wish-fulfilling jewel, all those resources and articles of enjoyment completely vanish. The divine wish-fulfilling jewel is firm, solid, and true; even a thousand *vajras* could not destroy it. Yet the resources and enjoyments it produced were false and impermanent, dispersing and perishing quickly."
"Consciousness is likewise firm and indestructible, yet the body it produces quickly decays and quickly perishes.
Great Medicine said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How can this supple and subtle consciousness penetrate into coarse and rigid matter?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!
The nature of water is extremely supple, yet its surging currents and suspended springs can pierce mountain rocks.
What do you think?
How do the qualities of hardness and softness compare between water and stone?
Mahābhaiṣajya said:
“World-Honored One!
The nature of stone is hard and rigid, like a diamond; the nature of water is soft and supple, providing all pleasant sensations.”
“Great Medicine! Consciousness is also like this:
most subtle and most supple, it can penetrate the form of the rigid and massive body, migrating into it to receive retribution.
Great Medicine again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When sentient beings cast off their bodies, how are they born among the various devas?
And how, up to the point of, are they born in places such as the hells?”
The Buddha said:
"Great Medicine!
When sentient beings approach the time of death, those who are supported by their meritorious karma cast off their ordinary vision and attain the wondrous vision of the gods."
With divine, wondrous vision, he beholds the six heavens of the desire realm; furthermore, he sees the bodies of beings in the six destinies moving about.
He sees celestial palaces, the Nandana Grove, and the Miśrakāvana Garden; he also sees the various devas dwelling in lotus halls, surrounded by beautiful maidens who laugh, jest, and play together.
Their ears are adorned with various flowers, they wear *kauśeya* garments, and their arms bear armlets.
Adorned with various kinds of bracelets and rings, with flowers perpetually in bloom and all requisites fully provided,
upon seeing the devas and devīs, their hearts become stained with attachment, filled with joy and satisfaction; their countenances are relaxed and pleasant like lotus flowers,
their gaze is steady and undistracted, their noses are neither deficient nor crooked, and their breath is not foul, while the color of their eyes is bright and fresh like the blue [lotus].
His body was like a lotus leaf; there was no pain in any of his joints, and no blood flowed from his eyes, ears, nose, or mouth.
He did not lose control of his excrement or urine, nor did his body hair stand on end or his pores become visible. His palms were not deathly yellow, nor were his nails bluish-black.
His hands and feet were neither disordered nor curled up; auspicious signs were clearly manifest.

He sees in the void of space a vast and lofty palace, with hundreds of thousands of variegated pillars arranged in exquisite array. Nets of bells hang down; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce a clear and delightful sound. Various fragrant flowers adorn the jeweled palace, and celestial youths, their bodies adorned with many jewels, sport within it. Having seen this, he feels joy, and as he smiles, his teeth appear like *kunda* flowers. His eyes are neither wide open nor closed; his voice is harmonious and smooth; his body is neither excessively cold nor excessively hot; though surrounded by his kinsmen, he feels no sorrow or distress. At the time when the sun first rises, he shall relinquish his life. What he perceives is bright and clear, free from all darkness, and a wondrous fragrance wafts from the four directions.

Seeing the sublime countenance of the Buddha, they felt joy and profound reverence; having seen him, they were filled with affection and delight. Their parting was like a brief departure, for they immediately returned to comfort their kin and acquaintances, ensuring they did not fall into distress. This is the natural law of the flowing stream of existence: birth is inevitably followed by death; do not give rise to suffering through conceptual discrimination.

“Mahābhaiṣajya! When a person of virtuous karma approaches the end of life, they delight in giving; they recite various gāthās and various verses of praise, and with various clarity and various proclamations, they expound the teachings of the True Dharma. Like one who is asleep yet not truly slumbering, they pass away in peace and tranquility.”

When he was about to relinquish his life-span, the celestial father and mother were seated together on one throne. From the hand of the celestial mother, flowers spontaneously emerged; seeing the flowers, she looked toward the celestial father and said:
"This is a most auspicious, rare, and excellent fruit. O Celestial One, you should know now that the time for your son’s joyful celebration will not be long."
The celestial mother then began to dangle the flower with both hands; as she was playing with it, her life came to an end.

Her formless consciousness abandoned the sense faculties, relinquished the objects and karma of the various realms, and cast off the affairs of those realms to migrate and receive a different retribution. It was like a rider dismounting one horse to mount another, like the sun’s rays drawing forth light, like fire produced from wood, or like the reflection of the moon appearing in clear water. Sustained by wholesome karma, the consciousness migrated to receive its celestial retribution, transferring into the flower as swiftly as the movement of wind through the channels.

The Heavenly Father and Mother sat together and gazed upon it; for seven days, the wind of desire and ambrosia blew over the flower. Adorned with precious earrings that shimmered and dazzled, a radiant and pure celestial youth appeared from the hand of the Heavenly Mother.
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can formless consciousness, by relying on the power of causes and conditions, give rise to that which has form?”
"How is it that that which has form abides within causes and conditions?
The Buddha said,
"Great Medicine!"

Just as fire is produced when pieces of wood come together and rub against one another, this fire cannot be found by searching within the wood; yet if the wood is removed, the fire likewise cannot be found. Fire arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and if these causes and conditions are not complete, the fire does not arise. Although the characteristic form of fire cannot ultimately be seen within the wood and other such materials, everyone nevertheless sees fire emerge from the wood.
Thus it is, Great Medicine!

Consciousness arises through the combination of the conditions of parents and other factors to produce a physical body; yet within the physical body, consciousness cannot be found, nor does consciousness exist apart from the physical body.
"O Mahauṣadha!
Just as when fire has not yet emerged, the signs of fire do not appear, and there is neither the sensation of heat nor any other characteristics;
even so, O Mahauṣadha!"
If the body does not yet exist, consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and volition do not manifest at all.
Great Medicine!

It is like seeing the brilliant radiance of the solar orb, yet ordinary people do not see the substance of the sun; they cannot know whether it is black, white, yellowish-white, or yellowish-red. They know that the sun exists only through its functions—its warming light, its rising and setting, and its circular movement.
"Consciousness is also like this; it is known to exist through its various activities.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying, "What are the activities of consciousness?"
The Buddha said:
"Great Medicine!
Feeling, perception, mental formations, volition, sorrow, suffering, and affliction—these are the functions of consciousness."
"Furthermore, there are wholesome and unwholesome karmas that, through perfuming, act as seeds and cause the manifesting consciousness to arise.
Great Medicine addressed the Buddha, saying:
