"How does consciousness, having departed from the body, swiftly take up another body? When consciousness has abandoned the old body but has not yet received the new body, what is the appearance of consciousness at that time?"
The Buddha said to Mahābhaiṣajya:

"Suppose there is a man with long arms, courageous and strong, clad in sturdy armor; he mounts a horse as swift as the wind and enters the fray. When the weapons clash, his mind becomes disordered and he falls from his horse, yet because he is so practiced in martial arts, he immediately leaps back onto it. In the same way, consciousness abandons the body and swiftly takes up another body."

Furthermore, just as a coward who, terrified upon seeing an enemy, flees on horseback, so too does consciousness, supported by wholesome karma, swiftly take rebirth in that realm upon seeing its celestial parents seated together.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
Regarding what you have asked: when consciousness has abandoned the old body but has not yet received a new body—at that moment, what are the characteristics of consciousness?
Mahābhaiṣajya!"

For example, when the reflection of a person appears in water, it has no substantiality that can be grasped; its hands, feet, face, eyes, and various features are no different from those of the person, yet the physical substance and activities of the body are entirely absent within the reflection. It is neither cold nor hot, nor does it possess any tactile sensations; it lacks fatigue, flesh, or the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). It is devoid of the sound of speech, the sound of the body, or sounds of pleasure and pain. Because consciousness has abandoned the old body and has not yet received the new body, its characteristics are likewise thus.
"Mahābhaiṣajya!
These are those who, having cultivated wholesome karma, are born among the devas.
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does consciousness arise in the hells?
The Buddha said,
“Great Medicine!
Those who have committed evil deeds enter hell; you should listen attentively! O Mahauṣadha!
Among these beings, having accumulated roots of unwholesomeness, at the time of their death they form this thought:
"I shall now die here; I am leaving behind my parents, kinsmen, and loved ones, which brings me great sorrow and suffering.

Seeing the various hells and seeing that his own body is destined to enter one of them, he sees his feet above and his head inverted and pointing downward. Furthermore, he sees a place where the ground is entirely blood; having seen this blood, his mind becomes attached to its taste. Due to the power of this mind of attachment, he is born in hell; through the causal force of the putrid, foul-smelling, and filthy water, consciousness takes up residence therein.
For example, just as insects are born within a place of filth and stench due to the causal power of various foul substances such as putrid curd and fermented wine,
so too do those who enter hell take birth by resorting to foul objects.
The youth Bhadrapāla, the Supreme and Excellent, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the physical appearances of the sentient beings in the hells?
Furthermore, what is their form?”

The Buddha said, “Great Medicine! Those who are born into the Blood-Soaked Earth Hell have bodies of blood-light, their forms the color of blood. Those born into the Boiling Moat have bodies like black clouds. Those born into the River of Milk-Broth have bodies with variegated spots of many colors; their bodies are extremely soft and fragile, like the body of a noble infant. Their height exceeds eight cubits, and their beards, hair, and body hairs are all long and trailing. Their hands, feet, faces, and eyes are deformed and incomplete; a person from Jambudvīpa would die upon seeing them from afar.”
Mahābhaiṣajya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What do the sentient beings in the hells take as food?
The Buddha said:

"Mahābhaiṣajya! The sentient beings in hell experience not even the slightest pleasure as they flee in terror. Seeing from afar molten copper and red liquid, they think it is blood and all rush toward it;
meanwhile, a voice cries out:
"May all those who are hungry come quickly to eat.

He then ran toward them; having arrived, he stood there with his hands cupped over his mouth. The hell-wardens poured hot molten copper into his cupped hands, forcing him to drink it. As the molten copper entered his belly, his bones and joints burst apart, and flames erupted from his entire body.
“Mahābhaiṣajya! Whatever food the beings in the hells consume only increases their suffering and provides not the slightest comfort.
Although the suffering of the hell-beings is such, consciousness does not abandon them, nor is it destroyed.”

Their bodies are like a heap of bones, and consciousness remains within them without departing; though their karmic retribution is exhausted, they do not abandon these suffering bodies. Pressed by the pains of hunger and thirst, they suddenly see gardens where flowers and fruits flourish in vast abundance and lush greenery.

Having seen this, they laugh with joy and say to one another: "These gardens are lush and verdant, with cool and beautiful breezes; let us all enter the gardens quickly for a brief moment of pleasure."

The leaves, flowers, and fruits of the trees all become swords and blades that hack and slice the offenders; some have their bodies split in two, while others cry out loudly and flee in all directions. Then the wardens of hell rise up in a crowd, wielding vajra-clubs, or iron maces, iron axes, and iron staves; biting their lips in rage, flames erupt from their bodies as they strike and beat the offenders, blocking them so they cannot escape—all of which arises from the offenders' own karma, causing them to perceive these things.
The hell-wardens followed behind the offenders and said to them:
"Where do you intend to go? You must stay here;
do not try to flee east or west—where do you hope to escape?"
"Now, this garden is adorned by your own karma; can you leave it? "It is so, Great Medicine!

The sentient beings in hell undergo various sufferings and die after seven days, only to be reborn in hell again. By the power of their karma, they are like wandering bees that, having gathered nectar from flowers, return to their original place."

Sentient beings with sinful karma who are destined for hell, at the moment of their initial death, see the messengers of death arrive; bound by the neck and driven forward, they experience great suffering of body and mind as they enter into profound darkness, like being seized and led away by bandits, crying out: "Alas! Woe is me!"

Alas! I now abandon my various beloved relatives and friends of Jambudvīpa to enter hell. I no longer see the path to heaven, but see only suffering; like a silkworm spinning its own thread to entangle itself until death, I have committed sins that bind me as an occupation, and with a lasso tied around my neck, I am dragged, driven, and coerced toward hell.
"O Bhadrapāla! Such is the nature of suffering for those born into the hells due to their sinful karma.
At that time, having heard these words, Bhadrapāla and Prince Mahauṣadha were struck with such terror that their hair stood on end; they rose together, joined their palms, and spoke as follows:

"We now all take refuge in the Buddha; we pray that you will grant us protection. We vow that by the merit of having heard this Dharma, until we have escaped the flow of existence and left the wheel of birth and death, may we not fall into the three miserable realms or enter hell."
Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to make a request; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
The Buddha said:
“As you desire, ask whatever you wish.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by "accumulation"?
What is meant by "heaping up"?
What is meant by "aggregate"?
"What is meant by 'the body does not transmigrate'?
The Buddha said, "Bhadrapāla!..."

The element of wisdom, the element of vision, the element of mind, and the element of clarity—by the combination of these four elements, a body is formed. The consciousness of the objects of these four elements is called "accumulation" (*caya*). "Aggregation" (*cita*) refers to the six elements and the six sense bases;

the six sense bases are the objects of the six consciousnesses, and the three elements are the cause of the two bases. That which arises from these causes—namely, hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, pus, blood, mucus, saliva, yellow phlegm, fat, grease, marrow, lymph, hands, feet, face, eyes, and the large and small joints—is a high accumulation through their combination, and is thus called an "aggregation. It is just as when grains, beans, sesame, and wheat are piled up and stored together until they become tall and large, which is called an "aggregation."
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are called the six elements (ṣaḍ-dhātu);
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are called the six bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana);

and visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are called the six objective fields (ṣaḍ-viṣaya). Furthermore, greed, hatred, and delusion are called the causes of the three realms.
Furthermore, wind, bile, and phlegm are also called the three causes.
The two causes for entry are ethical discipline and faith.
There are also two causes, namely equanimity and generosity.
Furthermore, there are two causes, namely vigor (*vīrya*) and concentration (*samādhi*). Again, there are two causes, namely the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

As for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*): these four are called the formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*). Feeling refers to the experiencing of the characteristics of pleasure and pain, as well as the characteristic of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Perception refers to the cognition of the characteristics of pleasure and pain. Formations refer to present mindfulness, attention (*manasikāra*), and contact (*sparśa*). Consciousness is the master of this body; it pervades all physical constituents, and there is nothing the body does that does not proceed from consciousness.

"Non-transmigration" refers to one who, having purified body, speech, and mind, realizes and attains the fruit of the Path; after this person dies, consciousness abandons the aggregates of existence (*bhava-skandha*), does not again undergo existence, and does not flow into the various realms of rebirth. Transmigrating to the Ultimate Bliss, they do not transmigrate again; this is called non-transmigration.
Thereupon, Bhadrapāla and Prince Mahauṣadha prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
This collection of teachings spoken by the Buddha, the All-Knowing One, shall bring great benefit, welfare, and happiness to sentient beings in the future.”

The Buddha said: “The Dharma-aggregate of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and not subject to annihilation; those who possess all-knowledge know this and do not act [to destroy it]. Having accumulated the light of wisdom through immeasurable diligent suffering, I now proclaim this sutra. This sun of the True Dharma shall provide great illumination for all sentient beings, and its virtuous renown shall flow everywhere into the ocean of omniscience. For those who can discipline the mind and maintain its flow, wherever this sutra is recited, explained, or taught, devas, ghosts and spirits, asuras, and mahoragas will all provide protection and come to pay homage. No fears of water, fire, kings, or thieves shall be able to harm them.”

"O Bhikṣus! From this day forward, do not preach this sutra before those who lack faith; be careful not to show it to those who seek out faults; do not preach it among the Nirgranthas, the followers of the Nirgrantha sect, or among other heterodox teachers; nor should you preach it to those who are disrespectful or who do not request it with longing.
If anyone violates my instruction and causes harm to the work of the Dharma, that person shall be considered one who harms the Tathāgata."

"O Bhikṣus! If there are those who pay homage to and make offerings to this sūtra, you should respectfully honor and provide for such persons; for these individuals are the upholders of the Tathāgatagarbha."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One should courageously transcend the burdens of worldly dust, Diligently cultivate the Buddha’s true teaching,
And utterly destroy the hosts of the army of death, Just as an elephant tramples through reeds and rushes."
"Uphold the Dharma and observe the precepts; with single-minded diligence, do not be negligent.
By doing so, you shall cast off the cycle of birth and death, exhausting all suffering and reaching its end.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Bhadrapāla-uttara, Prince Mahauṣadha, along with the assembly of bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and the rest of the great multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
